newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - KOREAN AIR.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - KOREAN AIR.

text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Confusion always reigns in the wake of a disaster and when a Korean airliner crashed into a hillside on the Pacific island of Guam last week, it reigned supreme.

While crash investigators were piecing together the final moments of the flight, insurers were desperately trying to assess which liability regime would come into play for compensation claims against them and the airline.

A number of questions were raised. Had Korean Air signed-up to the U.S. Department of Transport's compensation limits of special drawing rights (SDR) 250,000 per person? Was it aligned with Europe at SDR100,000? Or, had it abandoned limits to join the International Air Transport Association's Inter-Carrier Agreement (IATA ICA)?
The confusion was not because this was an Asian airliner flying into a U.S. territory, but simply because there is no global accord on liability.

In the event, all three regimes could apply. Korean Air's standard liability programme provided limits of SDR100,000, its U.S. flights were protected to SDR250,000 and it was a signatory to the IATA ICA.
The case highlights perfectly the need for consistency so insurers can begin to rate and reserve at appropriate levels.
IATA's move to consign the outdated Warsaw Convention to the history books was sensible. Its U.S.$75,000 limits had become meaningless, as had the loss estimates that were based on them.
The loss estimate is vital to risk rating. If estimates are held artificially low, insurers' calculations will never be realistic.
While the IATA ICA seeks to remove pre-determined limits, insurers would at least be able to use average liability loss statistics in rating calculations without challenge.

Initial balking at the removal of compensation limits has largely given way to the acceptance that it is better to start from this position rather than face the legal bills associated with defending the Warsaw Convention limits.
The task remains to get liability rates up to a suitable level -- vital as passenger volumes are set to soar with the introduction of 500-seat super-jumbos.
Insurers say the IATA ICA could add between US$100-US$300 million to the annual passenger liability claims bill, which has averaged US$400 million for each year of the 1990s.

Meanwhile rates softened by 15 to 20 percent at the last renewal and there are no signs that further softening can be avoided when renewal talks start again in October, even though 1997 is set to be one of the worst claims years on record.
Paradoxically insurers will be hoping the loss statistics provide a sufficiently disturbing picture to convince clients of the need to bring the global liability regime into line.
